\begin{bankpassage}[id=SI08-P1-CHEM-S3-G1-2, source={Score-I - Test 08 (09 Feb 2022)}, questions={1-2}]
Enthalpy of combustion of a given compounds is defined as following. It is the change in enthalpy when 1 mole of this compound combines with required amount of O$_2$ to give product in their stable forms. The enthalpy of combustion is usually measured by placing a known mass of the compound in a closed steel cointainer (known as bomb-calorimeter)

Given the data below :

$\Delta H^\circ_{\mathrm{comb}}(\mathrm{CH_4},\mathrm g)=-900$ kJ/mole;\par
$\Delta H^\circ_{\mathrm{comb}}(\mathrm C,\text{graphite})=-400$ kJ/mole

$\Delta H^\circ_{\mathrm{comb}}(\mathrm{H_2},\mathrm g)=-300$ kJ/mole ;\par
$\Delta H^\circ_{\mathrm{atomization}}(\mathrm C,\text{graphite})=700$ kJ/mole

and $\Delta H^\circ_{\mathrm f}(\mathrm H,\mathrm g)=200$ kJ/mole
\end{bankpassage}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SI09-P2-CHEM-S2-G7-8, source={Score-I - Test 09 (16 Feb 2022)}, questions={7-8}]
The amount of energy required to break a bond is same as the amount of energy released when the same bond is formed. In gaseous state, the energy required for \textit{homolytic cleavage} of a bond is called Bond Dissociation Energy (BDE) or Bond Strength. BDE is affected by $s$-character of the bond and the stability of the radicals formed. Shorter bonds are typically stronger bonds. BDEs for some bonds are given below :
\bfig{183.7}{SI09_p2_chem_s2_para7_8_1.png}
$\mathrm{Cl-Cl(g)\to Cl^{\bullet}(g)+Cl^{\bullet}(g)}$\quad $\Delta H^\circ=58$ kcal mol$^{-1}$\\
$\mathrm{H_3C-Cl(g)\to H_3C^{\bullet}(g)+Cl^{\bullet}(g)}$\quad $\Delta H^\circ=85$ kcal mol$^{-1}$\\
$\mathrm{H-Cl(g)\to H^{\bullet}(g)+Cl^{\bullet}(g)}$\quad $\Delta H^\circ=103$ kcal mol$^{-1}$
\end{bankpassage}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SII04-P1-CHEM-S2-G11-12, source={Score-II - Test 04 (07 May 2021)}, questions={11-12}]
The driving force $\Delta G$ diminishes to Zero on the way to equilibrium, first as in any other spontaneous process. Both $\Delta G$ and the corresponding cell potential $\left(E=\dfrac{-\Delta G}{nF}\right)$ are zero when the redox reaction comes to equilibrium. At equilibrium, the nernst equation is given as $E^0=\dfrac{0.059}{n}\log_{10}K$.
\end{bankpassage}

Enthalpy of neutralization is defined as the enthalpy change when 1gm equivalent of acid/base is completely neutralized by base/acid in dilute solution. For strong acid and strong base neutralization net chemical change is\\
H$^+$(aq) + OH$^-$(aq) $\rightarrow$ H$_2$O($\ell$) ;\\
$\Delta_rH^\circ=-55.84$kJ/mol \ $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{ionization}}$ of aqueous solution of strong acid and strong base is zero. When a dilute solution of a weak acid or based is neutralized, the enthalpy of neutralization is some what less because of the absorption of heat in the ionization of the weak acid or base, for weak acid/base\\
$\Delta H^\circ_{\text{neutralization}}=\Delta H^\circ_{\text{ionization}}+\Delta_rH^\circ(\text{H}^++\text{OH}^-\rightarrow\text{H}_2\text{O})$\\

\opt{C}{75 : 25}
\opt{D}{66.66 : 33.33}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=TOAS12-P2-CHEM-S2-G11-12, source={TOAS - Test 12 (10 Jul 2022)}, questions={11-12}]
Enthalpy of combustion of a given compounds is the change in enthalpy when 1 mole of this compound combines with required amount of O$_2$ to give product in their stable forms. The enthalpy of combustion is usually measured by placing a known mass of the compound in a closed steel container (known as bomb-calorimeter).
